about: Five epithets and one petition: fácere dignéris. Two of the five are words from Roman office and court: adscrípta means entered on a register, rata ratified; acceptábilis is the Church's own word, first found in Tertullian. The last petition before the consecration says outright what the offering is to become: Body and Blood. The sentence opens with the relative Quam, reaching back to the oblatiónem of Hanc ígitur — the two prayers are one run of thought.

s01.translation: Which oblation do thou, O God, we beseech thee, deign in all respects to make

s02.narrative: Three signs of the cross over the offerings.

s03.translation: blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable and acceptable:

s04.narrative: One sign of the cross over the host alone, at the word Corpus, and one over the chalice alone, at Sanguis.

s05.translation: that it may become for us the Body and Blood of thy most beloved Son our Lord Iesus Christ.

w001.function: The relative reaches back to the oblatiónem of the prayer before; Latin binds its paragraphs this way, where English starts a new sentence.

w003.function: A subject pronoun Latin usually leaves out: here it insists that God alone can do this.

w009.function: Literally entered on a list. The one word of the five the dictionaries do not head as an adjective — it is the perfect passive participle of adscríbo.

w010.function: The juridical epithet of the five: the offering is to be valid and irrevocable, as a ratified act (ratum habére).

w011.function: An echo of Rom 12:1: rationábile obséquium — a spiritual sacrifice, not an animal one.

w016.function: A dative of advantage: not in us but for us, to our benefit.

w017.function: Nominative: Corpus and Sanguis are the subjects of “fiat” (w020), though everything around them stands in other cases.

w020.function: Fio has almost all active forms with a passive meaning (the infinitive fíeri is the exception) — to become, that is, to be made; it serves as the passive of fácio.

w021.function: The superlative of the participle of díligo, to love by choice; in its positive degree the word the Father uses of the Son at the Jordan (diléctus).
